topics.label: Introduction and lecture framing
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture as an integration of previously introduced immune cells and molecules.

topics.label: Principles of innate recognition by pattern recognition receptors
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics establish how innate immune cells detect infection or damage through appropriately targeted and localised receptors.

topics.label: Toll-like receptor recognition and signalling
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how toll-like receptors translate microbial recognition into responses tailored to the location of the signal.

topics.label: Non-TLR recognition and inflammasome activation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics develop how recognition pathways beyond TLRs trigger inflammation that can become pathological.

topics.label: Sentinel-driven inflammation and leukocyte recruitment
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how activated sentinel cells generate inflammatory signals that mobilise immune cells to the infection site.

topics.label: Lymphatic drainage and adaptive immune priming
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how the lymphatic system carries evidence of tissue infection to lymph nodes to initiate adaptive immunity.

topics.label: Excessive systemic inflammation and septic shock
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic examines how an excessively activated inflammatory response produces life-threatening systemic effects.

topics.label: Passive and active resolution of inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how inflammatory activity subsides through the withdrawal of stimulation and the increasing action of inhibitory signals.

topics.label: Tissue repair and persistent inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine the limits of restoring inflamed tissue to homeostasis, with granulomas illustrating containment when an infection cannot be cleared.

topics.label: Lecture close and next lecture
topics.groupedBecause: This closing ends the lecture and identifies complement as the next lecture's subject.
